Preeti asked me again at the bus stop, "Nazia, are you okay? You've been so quiet." And I said, "I'm fine, just sleepy." That's the third time this week.
I'm not fine. She picked Rhea's group for the science project without even asking me, and then posted pictures of all of them at the café. I know it's small. I know she didn't mean it. But if I say it, she'll say sorry in that careful voice and it'll be weird on the bus for days.
So I smile and say fine. And she believes me, and we talk about the maths test instead, and it's okay. Except it isn't really okay. We used to tell each other everything. Now I have a whole list of things I haven't told her, and it keeps getting longer.
Maybe tomorrow. Maybe.

I told the girl next door her paintings were brilliant. I told the guys on my floor I loved their gaming nights. I told the seniors their band was great. I said "same here" to every opinion in the mess. None of it felt like lying. It felt like being easy to be around.

Wednesday. Nandini got her English test back: 11 out of 30. She folded it into a tiny square and pushed it to the bottom of her bag. At home, when Amma asked about the test, she said, "Not given back yet."
Friday. Her friend Kavitha said loudly on the school van, "Nandini, what did you get? I got 22." Nandini said, "I forgot to look." Kavitha frowned. Nandini's hands were cold. Now Kavitha might tell her mother, who might tell Amma.
The next Tuesday was parent-teacher day. Nandini lay awake the night before, heart pounding. In the morning, she took it out, smoothed it on the table, and said, "Amma, I lied. I got eleven." Amma looked at the paper, then at her face, and sat down beside her.

qa.q: What mark did Nandini get on her English test?
qa.a: She got 11 out of 30.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel on the night before parent-teacher day?
qa.a: She felt anxious and afraid, lying awake with her heart pounding because the hidden test and the lies were about to come out.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what finally helped?
qa.a: Each lie needed another one and made her fear grow; showing Amma the test herself ended the cover-up.

qa.q: What is it like for Kavitha when Nandini says she forgot to look?
qa.a: Kavitha finds it strange and is a little puzzled, because a test result is not something people usually forget.

grounding: It shows a child hiding a low mark and needing more lies over several days, with the fear growing each time until she tells the truth.

passage:
Siddharth, beta, you're hiding that report card like it's a snake. Come, let your Hafsa Nani tell you something.
When I was your size, I got a red mark in arithmetic. I was so ashamed that I tore the page out of my report book and hid it in the flour tin. Then my teacher asked why the page was missing, and I said my little brother tore it. Every day there was a new story to remember, and I shook whenever the flour tin was opened.
One morning my mother found the page, white with flour. She didn't shout. She only said, "You carried this alone for three weeks?" I cried from relief. The red mark was not half as heavy as the lies.

qa.q: Where did young Hafsa hide the torn page?
qa.a: She hid it in the flour tin.

qa.q: How did young Hafsa feel while the page was hidden?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and constantly frightened, shaking every time the flour tin was opened because of all the stories she had to keep straight.

qa.q: What turning point in the story ended her fear?
qa.a: When her mother found the page and asked gently instead of shouting, Hafsa could stop lying and finally felt relief.

qa.q: How might Hafsa's little brother have felt when she blamed him?
qa.a: He probably felt confused and unfairly accused, since he was pulled into a lie he knew nothing about.

grounding: A grandmother tells how a child's shame led to hiding a bad mark, and how each cover-up needed another lie until the truth brought relief.

passage:
Nilesh, you asked how I handled children who lie. In my third year of teaching, I, Rehana, was still young and impatient.
One boy in my class said his homework notebook had fallen into a drain. The same story, three times in a month. I wanted to shout. I had my ruler in my hand.
Instead, I put the ruler down and knelt beside his desk. I said quietly, "I think you're scared of what I'll say if the homework isn't done." He nodded.
"Thank you for telling me the real reason," I said. "Now let's see what part confused you."
It was fractions. After that, he never lost a notebook again. If I had punished him, he would only have learned to invent better drains.

qa.q: What did the boy say happened to his homework notebook?
qa.a: He said it had fallen into a drain.

qa.q: How was young Rehana feeling when she held the ruler?
qa.a: Rehana felt impatient and angry, tempted to shout because the same story came three times in a month.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed things?
qa.a: Rehana chose to kneel, name the boy's fear and thank him for the truth, which revealed that he was struggling with fractions.

qa.q: How might the boy have felt when Rehana named his fear?
qa.a: He likely felt relieved and understood, because someone saw the fear behind the lie instead of punishing it.

grounding: A retired teacher recalls staying calm, naming a child's fear and thanking him for the truth, making honesty cheaper than the cover-up.

The school van was already honking downstairs when Ramesh picked up Jahnavi's bag and felt how light it was.
"Where's your water bottle?"
"In the bag, Papa."
It wasn't. Jahnavi was staring at her shoes. It was the third bottle this term. Ramesh felt his voice rising. The van honked again.
He stopped, crouched to her level and spoke quietly. "Jahnavi, I think you're worried I'll be angry about the bottle."
She nodded, eyes wet. "I left it in the park yesterday. I'm sorry."
"Thank you for telling me the truth. That matters more than any bottle." He pushed an old plastic one into her bag. "We'll look in the park after school, together."
She ran down the stairs, lighter than her bag.

qa.q: Where did Jahnavi say she left the bottle?
qa.a: She said she left it in the park yesterday.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi say the bottle was in the bag?
qa.a: She was scared that Papa would be angry about losing a third bottle, so the lie was a quick way to avoid that moment.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do well under time pressure?
qa.a: He stopped, crouched, named her worry and thanked her for the truth, then solved the problem quickly with another bottle.

qa.q: What would change if Ramesh had shouted as the van honked?
qa.a: Jahnavi would probably learn to hide things better next time, and the truth about the park would stay buried.

grounding: It shows a parent staying calm under time pressure, naming the fear behind a child's lie and thanking her for the truth.

From the balcony of their Salt Lake flat, Rekha saw the neighbour's scooter mirror lying on the ground, a cricket ball beside it.
Arnab came in soon after, sweaty and too quiet.
"Did your ball hit Mr. Dutta's scooter?"
"No, Ma. Some older boys were playing."
Rekha remembered how her own father used to hit first and ask later, and how well she had learned to lie. She patted the sofa cushion.
"Arnab, you look frightened. I think you're scared I'll be angry about the mirror."
After a long moment he said, "It was my shot. Sorry."
"Thank you for telling me. That was harder than the shot." She held his hand. "Now let's go down together and tell Mr. Dutta."

qa.q: What was lying on the ground near the scooter?
qa.a: The neighbour's scooter mirror was lying on the ground, with a cricket ball beside it.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he came in too quiet?
qa.a: He was frightened and guilty, worried his mother would be angry about the broken mirror.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that made the truth easier?
qa.a: She stayed calm, named his fear, thanked him for being honest, and then went with him to tell Mr. Dutta.

qa.q: Why might Rekha react differently from her own father?
qa.a: She remembers that being hit first taught her only to lie better, so she wants Arnab to feel safe telling the truth.

grounding: It shows a parent staying calm, naming a child's fear and thanking him for the truth, knowing harsh punishment teaches concealment.

It was the night before the chemistry board practical, and Ankita's phone buzzed on the study table. Mohit: "Need my notes back tmrw, sorry!" Her mother looked up from the sofa.
"Who is it?"
"Megha," Ankita said. "Group project." Her heart thumped.
Last year, when she had mentioned Mohit helping her in class, her father had read her chats aloud at dinner and her mother had laughed about "boyfriends." She had cried in the bathroom. Since then she had kept Mohit's messages to herself.
Now the lie was growing. Tomorrow she would have to hand him the notes at the gate, where her mother dropped her.
She lay awake, tired and cross with herself. She didn't want to be a liar. She just wanted one thing that wasn't turned into a joke. In the morning, she decided, she'd talk to her school counsellor about how to tell her parents.

qa.q: What did Ankita say when her mother asked who texted?
qa.a: She said, "Megha. Group project."

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling as she lay awake?
qa.a: She felt tired, cross with herself and anxious, not wanting to be a liar but afraid her friendship would be mocked again.

qa.q: What wise step did Ankita choose instead of building more lies?
qa.a: She decided to talk to her school counsellor about how to tell her parents, which gets a trusted adult's help.

qa.q: How might Ankita's parents see things if they knew why she hid the friendship?
qa.a: They might realise their ridicule and chat-reading made the truth feel unsafe, rather than blaming only Ankita's character.

grounding: It shows a teenager hiding a friendship because past honesty led to ridicule and control, and the lie reflecting how unsafe the truth felt.

Every night after ten, when the flat went quiet, Wasim slid his phone under the quilt and opened a chess app to play a game with Siddharth, his friend from the Bandra chess club.
He had told his father about the club once, last winter. His father had laughed in front of the relatives. "Chess? You can't even win at carrom." Then the phone got a lock only his father knew.
So Wasim used the old phone his cousin had left behind, and now he played in secret. When his father asked why he was sleepy in the mornings, Wasim said, "Studying late." Each time, he felt a little sick.
One night Siddharth texted: "Tournament on Sunday. You coming?" Wasim stared at the screen. Going meant another lie, a bigger one.
He typed, "Can't." Then deleted it. Maybe his mother would listen, if he told her first.

qa.q: What did Wasim's father say when he heard about the chess club?
qa.a: He laughed and said, "Chess? You can't even win at carrom."

qa.q: How does Wasim feel each time he says "Studying late"?
qa.a: Each time he feels a little sick, guilty about the lie but afraid of being laughed at again.

qa.q: What small step could help Wasim stop hiding?
qa.a: Telling his mother first, as he is considering, could get a trusted adult on his side before talking to his father.

qa.q: What would change if Wasim's father had listened instead of laughing last winter?
qa.a: Wasim might have shared the tournament openly, because the truth would have felt safe instead of embarrassing.

grounding: It shows a teenager hiding phone use because past honesty led to ridicule and control, showing that the lie reflects how unsafe truth felt.

"Why do you keep flipping your phone over whenever Chachi walks in?" Mahima asked, sitting down next to her younger cousin on the terrace.
"No reason," Arnab said.
"Arnab. I'm your didi. Try again."
He picked at the edge of his slipper. "You know Riju, from the next colony? We message about football."
"So?"
"Last time I told Ma I had a new friend, she checked all my messages. Then she told the whole family I was 'getting into bad company.' Everyone laughed at dinner."
Mahima was quiet. "That sounds horrible."
"So now I just don't tell her anything."
"And how does that feel?"
"Tiring. Like I'm always hiding."
"Do you want me to sit with you when you talk to Chachi? You don't have to do it alone."
Arnab let out a long breath. "Maybe. Yes."

qa.q: Where were Mahima and Arnab sitting?
qa.a: They were sitting on the terrace.

qa.q: What does Arnab's picking at his slipper suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt embarrassed and uneasy, not sure it was safe to tell even his didi about Riju after the family had laughed at him.

qa.q: How did Mahima support Arnab?
qa.a: She listened without judging and offered to sit with him when he talks to his mother, so he doesn't have to do it alone.

qa.q: How does Mahima see Arnab's secrecy after hearing the story?
qa.a: She sees it as a reaction to being mocked and checked, not as bad character, which is why she calls it horrible and offers help.

grounding: It shows a teenager hiding a friendship because past honesty led to checking and ridicule, and a cousin helping him move toward safer honesty.

The paddy was nearly cut, and the whole village near Champhai had come to help Lalremsiami's family bring in the harvest. Lalremsiami's father told everyone at the tea break, "My daughter has passed all her nursing papers. First class!"
Lalremsiami smiled and handed around the cups. She had failed two papers in the last semester. She had written "passed" in her messages home, and it had seemed easier than hearing her father go quiet on the phone.
That evening her college friend Sarita called. "The re-exam form closes on Friday. Did you fill it?"
"Not yet."
"Siami, you have to. And your family?"
"They think I passed."
Sarita was silent a moment. "Every week it gets bigger."
Lalremsiami looked out at her father laughing by the fire. She felt the trap close a little more.

qa.q: How many papers had Lalremsiami failed?
qa.a: She had failed two papers in the last semester.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she looked at her father laughing by the fire?
qa.a: She felt trapped and guilty, afraid of disappointing him yet aware that each week the false story grew.

qa.q: What would you advise Lalremsiami to do next?
qa.a: Fill in the re-exam form before Friday and tell her family the truth soon, perhaps with a trusted relative or Sarita's support.

qa.q: How does Sarita see the situation?
qa.a: Sarita sees the lie growing every week and worries about her friend, which is why she reminds her about the form and the family.

grounding: It shows a student in a proud family claiming to have passed while quietly failing, and the gap between story and reality becoming a trap.

On Sunday video calls, Javier's parents in Valencia always asked about the internship. "It's going well," he said every week, sitting in front of the same bookshelf in his Madrid room. There was no internship. He had failed two exams in January and spent the spring retaking them.
His flatmate Amara sometimes heard the calls through the thin wall. One evening she knocked. "Your mum just told my mum on the group chat that they're flying up for your 'end of internship' dinner."
Javier's face went grey. "When?"
"The fifteenth."
He sat on the bed. "I didn't want them to think they wasted all that money on me."
Amara sat beside him. "They'll be more hurt that you carried this alone. Call them tonight. I'll stay in the kitchen if you want someone nearby."
He picked up his phone.

qa.q: Where do Javier's parents live?
qa.a: They live in Valencia.

qa.q: How did Javier feel when Amara told him about the dinner?
qa.a: He felt panicked and ashamed, his face going grey, because the false story he told to avoid disappointing his parents was about to collapse.

qa.q: What could fix the situation, as Amara suggests?
qa.a: Calling his parents that night and telling them the truth, with Amara nearby, before the trip makes it bigger.

qa.q: How might Javier's parents feel if they arrived for a dinner that isn't real?
qa.a: They would likely feel shocked and hurt, more by being kept in the dark than by the failed exams.

grounding: It shows a student hiding failure from parents with a false internship story until the gap between story and reality becomes a trap.
